definition: Empirical relationships describing how model performance improves predictably as a function of model size, dataset size, and compute used for training.
details: Scaling laws have guided decisions about how to allocate compute budgets between larger models versus more training data, and were pivotal in motivating the trend toward ever-larger language models.

explainer.lead: Scaling laws are empirical relationships describing how model performance improves predictably with model size, dataset size, and training compute. They matter because they have guided how compute budgets are split between bigger models and more training data, and motivated the trend toward ever-larger language models.

tiers.eli5: It's like a rule of thumb that says if you make the recipe bigger and cook it longer, the dish reliably gets better in a predictable way.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use scaling laws to decide whether extra compute is better spent on a larger model or on more training data. A pitfall is treating an empirical trend as a guarantee beyond the regimes where it was measured.
tiers.paperLevel: They are empirical relationships between performance and model size, dataset size and training compute; being empirical, they describe observed trends rather than guaranteeing behaviour outside measured conditions.

explainer.example: A team with a fixed compute budget uses scaling-law estimates to compare the expected performance of a larger model trained on less data against a smaller model trained on more.

citation.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
